commenti.body: Great movie. I think the whole thing is a part of the cycle of self-defensive rebirth that we see in action. The movie opens with the same highway that happens right before the identity switch - what’s to say that was the first time it happened? Could be that Bill Pullman is as much a projection as Balthazar Getty. There’s a really enjoyable podcast episode about it from [best little horror house in Philly](https://open.spotify.com/episode/2F2tF8M52vJ10SDFlGkBE3?si=q1W4TgTlQuOPdzwHualRDg)

Just did my second watch of this last friday, I loved my second watch and getting to see clues that fit what i thought was happening (most likely confirmation bias 😅)


I interpret it a similar way as Mulholland drive, that scenes are either brain logic true without much of the truth of the heart, or emotionally true without being "real".


I think a big indicator of this lies in the sex scenes. Fred has awkward sex, which stems from sexual inadequacy or feelings of sexual inadequacy. This leads to him letting in the mystery man, who I believe represents the evil he let in through his mind through jealousy and shame. And this evil takes over and he kills his wife. These scenes are given to us with a slight distortion on reality, but mostly really happened. You don't see much emotion or passion from him or Alice, the relationship is emotionally stunted and cold, no real communication. He doesnt remember because he lets the evil run the show.


The rest of the movie is a delusional fantasy, with his shame and bleak reality breaking through the veneer of the delusion. He's young, virile, a stud, having passionate sex with multiple partners. His life is exciting and dangerous and driven by passion. But that shame of reality keeps rearing it's head.


I love this movie, and I especially love that I'm probably wrong about all of this!

To me the film takes place in the subconscious of the main character, where Fred and Pete are two different aspects of the same person. Fred represents what he fears that he is, insecure and unable to sexually satisfy a woman. Pete is who he wishes he could be, a young man who gets down with the ladies without any effort.

The same can be said for the female characters, Renee is what he fears women think of him, while Alice is his idea of the perfect woman. His jealousy and insecurity lead him to kill Renee and escape what he has become by turning into Pete, a man worthy of being with the ideal woman. This ideal however, starts falling apart once he finds out about her past sexual experiences. This once again awakens his feelings of sexual inadequacy, and when he finally is told that he can never have Alice, he ultimately turns back into Fred.

The final scene on the highway is him turning back and forth between these two characters presumably forever.

A final note is that although the film is viewed through the eyes of an unreliable narrator, there is an interesting scene where Fred explains why he doesn't like cameras:

>"I like to remember things my own way... How I remembered them... Not necessarily the way they happened".

This could indicate that what we see on video tapes, is a more objective view of who he really is.

This is obviously just one of many possible interpretations, and it still leaves a lot of questions unanswered, such as Mr. Eddy/Dick Laurent and the mystery man.

Firstly, I love Lost Highway! It has been completely overshadowed by Mulholland Dr., but I actually prefer LH (although I like them both).

Unlike with Mulholland Dr., I don't think there is any way to reduce Lost Highway in a satisfying way into anything more coherent than dream logic (and perhaps that's why Mulholland Dr. found much more acclaim and a much larger audience).

Not only does he imagine himself as Pete, a cool guy with several beautiful partners, but he also inserts Alice into his fantasy as a mafia porn star who was about to run away with some guy. This delusion helps him justify the murder to himself.

Like most Lynch movies, I've seen it three times over the past 20 years, roughly spaced 10 years between. I watched it some time ago. 

My takeaway was that Fred, feeling older, weak, and insecure/jealous from his inability to appease his wife (sexually, emotionally), subconsciously wants to be a cool young stud (Pete the methanic) that's popular among the ladies, even his own wife. Maybe that's who Fred once was, in his younger days when he met his wife? Fred now lives a cold, unfulfilled life - I think the avantgarde jazz indicates that there's little harmony in his life.  

I always thought that Mystery Man and Mr. Eddy / Dick Laurent represented his consciousness and ideal. Mystery Man is the weak evil inside him - he's short, pale, hairless - looks like a ghoul basically, while Mr. Eddy is some kind of strong, disciplined man with integrity. He's large, strong, swaggering and loud (while Dick Laurent is some infamous mobster/criminal in the world of Fred). Lynch has a thing for internal good and evil.

**So, how does this all tie up? (spoilers ahead)** 

Fred, tired of suspecting his wife of infidelity, finally snaps and kills her. Leading up to this we get the hints that Mystery Man has entered their home, and thus Fred. - which is shown through the video tapes, meeting at the party. 

Unable to cope with the fact that he actually killed her, he takes on the personality of a person he wishes to be. This is through trauma, and IIRC, Lynch had used some mental illness as the direct inspiration for this. 

With a "fresh start" as Pete, he has a good relationship with the strong and idealized Mr. Eddy (Dick Laurent) - but is also taken by Alice, the idealized version of his wife, who he also knows is off limits - being Dick's girl. This is Fred (through Pete) wanting his own wife, but being fearful that he's not a "man enough", as she is already taken by his idealized character - but who he cannot be. 

Throughout their affair Pete learns that Alice is being forced to partake in porn shoots etc., and that she wants out. I take this as Fred trying to rationalize her infidelity - that it was not due to him (sexual impotence, jealousy, etc.), but some other external factor - she was forced. 

When they make a run for it, Pete encounters a bunch of hints from his previous life. The photo where Alice and Renee are together, his phone call with both Dick / Mr. Eddy and the Mystery Man. In the end, Fred becomes Pete again - maybe due to all the hints - and is told by Alice that he will never be hers. The illusion is shattered. 

Mystery Man appears again, which symbolizes the evil taking over / guiding Fred. They find Dick, which ends up with evil literally killing the good - when Mystery Man shoots Dick. 

Fred drives home and says to himself "Dick Laurent his dead", through intercom, which symbolizes that evil has won - and sets of the events in the beginning of the movie. 

Fred finds himself caught up with moral (law enforcement) and tries to run away from it. Reality sets in, and he's taken back to his cell again. Some like to say that he's probably being executed in the electric chair, and that he can't escape judgement for his actions. 

--- 

As with all Lynch movies, there's no single way to analyze this. And I'm probably forgetting a bunch of details. 

But to me, it is the story of a insecure man who's battling the good and evil within, and ultimately loses to evil.

There is a theory that Pete is a manifestation of Fred's absolutely desperate desire to escape from the dire situation he's in.

His transformation into Pete literally gets him out of prison!

It was a really smart move to use Arquette to play both Rene and Alice, as it connects the first two acts of the film perfectly.

So many films these days, I find, fail to provide a satisfying conclusion to the set up. In this case, Fred delivering that final line ties up the film beautifully.

Lost Highway really is a masterpiece.
